# SK2220 — The conditionally compiled call sits under a directive that deletes it

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A call to a [Conditional("X")] method stands inside a preprocessor branch that was taken because X is not defined, so the compiler deletes the call here and the build that defines X never compiles the statement at all.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

`[Conditional("DEBUG")]` deletes the call site in every compilation that does not define `DEBUG`. Writing that call inside `#if !DEBUG` therefore produces a statement that runs in no configuration whatever: where `DEBUG` is undefined the directive admits it and the attribute removes it, and where `DEBUG` is defined the directive excludes it before the compiler sees it. The two mechanisms cancel. Somebody wrote both, so somebody meant the call to happen — and it never does, in any build, on any machine.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
#if !DEBUG
    Log.Trace("release only");   // Log.Trace is [Conditional("DEBUG")]
#endif
```

Write:

```csharp
#if DEBUG
    Log.Trace("debug only");
#endif
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The evidence is the branch the preprocessor took, never the compilation's symbol list.** Reading `PreprocessorSymbolNames` directly would report every `Debug.Assert` in every release build — which is `[Conditional]` doing exactly its job and is not a defect at all. What makes this shape a defect is that somebody wrote a guard stating they expected the call to run here, and the guard and the attribute contradict each other.

⚠ **The redundant sibling shape is not this rule, and the reason is structural rather than a matter of taste.** `[Conditional("DEBUG")]` called inside `#if DEBUG` duplicates what the attribute already does and breaks nothing; belt and braces is a legitimate style. It is also unobservable from any compilation that does not define the symbol, because that region is disabled text holding no invocation node to analyse. Only one of the two shapes is ever visible in one compilation, and which one is decided by the symbol's absence. This rule takes the shape that is a defect *and* visible in the same compilation that proves it.

⚠ **Every one of the method's `[Conditional]` symbols must be proved undefined.** The attribute is additive: a method carrying both `[Conditional("DEBUG")]` and `[Conditional("TRACE")]` survives when *either* symbol is defined, so proving one absent proves nothing about the call. A rule that matched the first attribute and stopped would report a live call as dead, which is the worst thing a correctness rule can say. The attribute is read from the method and from every definition it overrides, and an attribute argument that is not a constant string withdraws the finding.

⚠ **Two directive shapes are read and no others.** `#if !X` whose branch was taken proves `X` undefined; the `#else` of a plain `#if X` proves the same. `#elif` chains, `&&`, `||`, parentheses and comparisons are all declined, because each can be true for reasons that say nothing about one symbol. Only a statement whose entire content is the call is reported, so the fix has a deletion that leaves the rest of the expression standing — a `[Conditional]` method returns `void`, so this is the shape such a call almost always has. Generated code is excluded.

⚠ **The fix is not marked safe even though the edit is behaviour-identical.** Deleting the statement removes text the compiler already removes, so nothing observable changes. What a review still has to decide is whether the directive was the typo: an author who wrote `#if !DEBUG` and meant `#if DEBUG` wants the guard corrected, not the call deleted, and an unreviewed fix would quietly settle that question the wrong way.
